metadata.name: sudo
metadata.displayName: sudo - Execute commands as another user

installation.note: sudo is installed by default on most Linux distributions (Ubuntu, Debian, etc.)

overview.summary: sudo (superuser do) allows a permitted user to execute commands as another user, typically the root user. It's the safe way to perform administrative tasks without logging in as root. sudo provides an audit trail of all commands executed.

misconceptions.title: sudo uses root password
misconceptions.reality: sudo prompts for YOUR password, not root's password. This is a key security feature - you don't need to know root's password.
misconceptions.tip: sudo uses your password. If you don't have sudo access, ask your administrator to add you to the sudoers group.

misconceptions.title: sudo is the same as su
misconceptions.misconception: sudo and su work the same way
misconceptions.reality: sudo executes a single command as another user. su switches to another user's shell. sudo is generally preferred for security and audit trails.
misconceptions.tip: Use sudo for single commands. Use su only when you need to run multiple commands as another user.

common_pitfalls.description: Running commands with sudo that don't need root access
common_pitfalls.solution: Only use sudo when necessary. Regular file operations in your home directory don't need sudo. Check if command works without sudo first.

common_pitfalls.description: Forgetting that sudo caches password for 15 minutes
common_pitfalls.solution: sudo caches your password for 15 minutes (default). After that, you'll be prompted again. Use sudo -k to invalidate immediately.

common_pitfalls.description: Getting 'user is not in sudoers file' error
common_pitfalls.solution: Ask your system administrator to add you to the sudoers group: sudo usermod -aG sudo username (requires root access to run this).

related_commands.relationship: Configure sudo; edit sudoers file safely

best_practices: Only use sudo when necessary - don't use it for regular file operations
Read commands carefully before entering password - typos can be dangerous
Use sudo -v to extend session if you're doing multiple sudo commands
Use sudo -u to run commands as specific users when needed
Check if command works without sudo first
Be careful with destructive commands (rm, dd, etc.) when using sudo
performance_tips: sudo is fast - password caching makes subsequent commands instant
Use sudo -v to extend session before running multiple sudo commands

additional_notes.password_caching: sudo caches your password for 15 minutes (default). After that, you'll be prompted again.
additional_notes.security: sudo provides audit trail - all sudo commands are logged in /var/log/auth.log
additional_notes.sudoers: User permissions are configured in /etc/sudoers (edit with visudo, never directly)
additional_notes.vs_su: sudo is preferred over su for security - it provides better audit trails and doesn't require root password
additional_notes.common_use: Most common pattern: sudo apt install package, sudo systemctl restart service, sudo nano /etc/file
